newsitem.title: USA: Florida trio get 15 years in stop sign theft case.
newsitem.headline: Florida trio get 15 years in stop sign theft case.

text.p: A Florida judge on Friday sentenced three friends to 15 years each in prison on manslaughter convictions for the theft of a stop sign that led to an accident in which three teenagers were killed.
Christopher Cole and Thomas Miller, 20, and Nissa Baillie, 21, were convicted last month of stealing the sign from an intersection near Tampa in February 1996.
It is believed to be the first U.S. case in which there was a manslaughter conviction for the theft of a traffic sign.
The three defendants denied that they stole the sign where the accident took place, but admitted they stole other signs as a prank. They were arrested while throwing stolen signs into a river.
Kevin Farr, Brian Hernandez and Randall White, all 18, were killed when they rode through the intersection, unaware there had been a stop sign, into the path of a semi trailer truck.

Hillsborough County Judge Bob Anderson Mitcham could have sent the three to jail for as much as 50 years. He said he imposed lesser sentences because he did not believe the defendants intended to harm anyone.

"But the acts that you did caused the deaths of these three young people," Mitcham told the defendants. "There must be some punishment in this case. You will for the rest of your lives live with this tragedy."
Relatives of the three victims had urged the judge to impose stiff sentences, while relatives of the defendants asked for leniency.
"I ask that you give the maximum penalty that's allowable. I think my son and the two other individuals received the maximum," Les Farr, father of Kevin Farr, told the judge.
"We have never seen any remorse from any of these defendants," added prosecutor Leland Baldwin.
Both Cole and Baillie cried as the judge imposed their sentences. All three defendants were handcuffed and were dressed in prison uniforms.

Before imposing the sentences, Mitcham denied a motion for a new trial. The defendants had argued on Thursday that their convictions should be overturned because a key prosecution witness, Larry Jarrard, recanted his testimony.
Jarrard testified on Thursday that he lied at the trial when he said the defendants told him they took the stop sign the day before the accident because he was threatened by Baldwin.
She denied making any threats against Jarrard.
Mitcham ruled there was enough evidence to convict the defendants without Jarrard's testimony.
Mitcham granted bond to the three pending appeals of their convictions; $50,000 each for Cole and Baillie and $60,000 for Miller, who had a prior criminal record.
